steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the "Limitations" section of an encyclopedia article on air gaps in computer networking, covering the restrictions placed on devices and the known attacks that have defeated air-gapped isolation.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Restrictions on devices in air-gapped environments
- Air-gapped networks still vulnerable
- Timeline of demonstrated attacks (2013-2018)
- General picture: air-gap covert channels and media

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Restrictions
  - ban on wireless connections to/from secure network
  - restrictions on EM leakage: TEMPEST, Faraday cage
- Still vulnerable despite no direct connection
- Attacks
  - 2013: acoustic signaling air gap malware shown viable; then Dragos Ruiu's BadBIOS gets press attention
  - 2014: AirHopper, bifurcated attack, isolated computer -> nearby mobile phone via FM signals
  - 2015: BitWhisper, covert channel between air-gapped computers via thermal manipulation; bidirectional, no extra dedicated peripheral hardware
  - later 2015: GSMem, exfiltration over cellular frequencies; standard internal bus -> small cellular transmitter antenna
  - 2016: ProjectSauron discovered, undetected 5 years; infected USB device leaks data off air-gapped computer
    - multiple infection media; hidden USB partitions not visible to Windows as transport channel to internet-connected computer, presumably for file sharing
  - 2018: NFCdrip, stealthy exfiltration via NFC radio abuse and signal detection; NFC normally within a few centimeters, shown up to 100 meters
- General
  - malware exploits hardware combinations: "air-gap covert channels"
  - media: acoustic, light, seismic, magnetic, thermal, radio-frequency

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Devices used in these environments may have limitations, like a ban on wireless connections to or from the secure network, or similar restrictions on EM leakage from the secure network by using TEMPEST or a Faraday cage.

Even though they have no direct connection to other systems, air-gapped networks have been shown to be vulnerable to attack in different circumstances.

In 2013 scientists showed that air gap malware made to defeat air-gapped isolation using acoustic signaling was viable. Soon after, BadBIOS, by network security researcher Dragos Ruiu, got attention in the press.

In 2014 researchers introduced AirHopper, a bifurcated attack pattern that showed data could be exfiltrated from an isolated computer to a mobile phone nearby using FM frequency signals.

In 2015 BitWhisper was introduced, which is a covert signaling channel between air-gapped computers that uses thermal manipulations. BitWhisper supports communication in both directions and needs no extra dedicated peripheral hardware.

- Later 2015: GSMem, data exfiltration from air-gapped computers over cellular frequencies; transmission generated by standard internal bus turns computer into small cellular transmitter antenna
- 2016: ProjectSauron discovered after 5 years undetected; infected USB device leaks data off air-gapped computer
  - multiple infection media; one used hidden partitions on USB drive not visible to Windows as transport channel to an internet-connected computer, presumably to share files
- 2018: NFCdrip, stealthy exfiltration through NFC radio abuse and signal detection
  - NFC normally needs devices within a few centimeters; shown to work up to 100 meters
- General: malware uses hardware combinations, "air-gap covert channels"
  - media: acoustic, light, seismic, magnetic, thermal, radio-frequency

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Devices used in these environments may have limitations, like a ban on wireless connections to or from the secure network, or similar restrictions on EM leakage from the secure network by using TEMPEST or a Faraday cage.

Even though they have no direct connection to other systems, air-gapped networks have been shown to be vulnerable to attack in different circumstances.

In 2013 scientists showed that air gap malware made to defeat air-gapped isolation using acoustic signaling was viable. Soon after, BadBIOS, by network security researcher Dragos Ruiu, got attention in the press.

In 2014 researchers introduced AirHopper, a bifurcated attack pattern that showed data could be exfiltrated from an isolated computer to a mobile phone nearby using FM frequency signals.

In 2015 BitWhisper was introduced, which is a covert signaling channel between air-gapped computers that uses thermal manipulations. BitWhisper supports communication in both directions and needs no extra dedicated peripheral hardware.

Later in 2015 researchers introduced GSMem, a way to exfiltrate data from air-gapped computers over cellular frequencies. The transmission is generated by a standard internal bus and turns the computer into a small cellular transmitter antenna.

ProjectSauron malware was discovered in 2016 after it had stayed undetected for 5 years, and it shows how an infected USB device can be used to leak data remotely off an air-gapped computer. The malware came from several infection media. One of them used hidden partitions on a USB drive, not visible to Windows, as a transport channel between the air-gapped computer and a computer connected to the internet, presumably to share files between the two systems.

NFCdrip was the name for the discovery in 2018 of stealthy data exfiltration through NFC (Near-field communication) radio abuse and signal detection. NFC lets devices communicate effectively by bringing them within a few centimeters of each other, but researchers showed it can be abused to send information much further than expected, up to 100 meters.

In general, malware can use different hardware combinations to leak sensitive information from air-gapped systems using "air-gap covert channels". These hardware combinations bridge the air-gap with a number of different media, including acoustic, light, seismic, magnetic, thermal, and radio-frequency.

steps.text:
Limitations imposed on devices used in these environments may include a ban on wireless connections to or from the secure network, or similar restrictions on EM leakage from the secure network through the use of TEMPEST or a Faraday cage.

Despite having no direct connection to other systems, air-gapped networks have been shown to be vulnerable to attack in various circumstances.

In 2013, scientists demonstrated the viability of air gap malware designed to defeat air-gapped isolation using acoustic signaling. Shortly after, network security researcher Dragos Ruiu's BadBIOS received press attention.[1]

In 2014, researchers introduced AirHopper, a bifurcated attack pattern showing that data can be exfiltrated from an isolated computer to a nearby mobile phone using FM frequency signals.[2,3]

In 2015, BitWhisper, a covert signaling channel between air-gapped computers using thermal manipulations, was introduced. BitWhisper supports bidirectional communication and requires no additional dedicated peripheral hardware.[4,5]

Later in 2015, researchers introduced GSMem, a method for exfiltrating data from air-gapped computers over cellular frequencies. The transmission, generated by a standard internal bus, turns the computer into a small cellular transmitter antenna.[6,7]

The discovery of ProjectSauron malware in 2016, after it had remained undetected for 5 years, demonstrates how an infected USB device can be used to remotely leak data off of an air-gapped computer.[8] The malware came from multiple infection media, one of which relied on hidden partitions on a USB drive, not visible to Windows, as a transport channel between the air-gapped computer and a computer connected to the internet, presumably as a way to share files between the two systems.[9]

NFCdrip was the name given to the discovery of stealthy data exfiltration through NFC (Near-field communication) radio abuse and signal detection in 2018. Although NFC lets devices establish effective communication by bringing them within a few centimeters of each other,[10] researchers showed that it can be abused to transmit information at a much longer range than expected - up to 100 meters.[11]

In general, malware can exploit various hardware combinations to leak sensitive information from air-gapped systems using "air-gap covert channels".[12] These hardware combinations use a number of different media to bridge the air-gap, including acoustic, light, seismic, magnetic, thermal, and radio-frequency.[13,14,15]
